current_proposition: For cycle tracking, Day 1 is the first day of menstrual bleeding; the cycle is counted from that day to the first day of the next period.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Sections: What is the menstrual cycle? / How long is a typical menstrual cycle?
evidence_summary: OWH: cycle 'begins with the first day of menstruation and continues until the next period starts.' Directly confirms Day-1 counting convention.
scope_restrictions: General educational tracking convention, not a diagnostic claim.

current_proposition: In adults, menstrual cycle length normally varies across people and can vary over time. Niswah should present any source-specific numeric range only with its source and population context, not as a universal diagnostic boundary.
independent_corroborating_source: NICHD (21-35d, teens 21-45d) AND ACOG FAQ 'Your First Period'/'Abnormal Uterine Bleeding' (21-45d broad, 21-35d typical) both independently checked
relevant_section_heading_locator: Section: How long is a typical menstrual cycle? (24–38 days in this source)
evidence_summary: OWH states 24-38 days; NICHD states 21-35 (most women) / 21-45 (teens); ACOG states 21-45 broad, 21-35 typical. All three institutions agree cycles vary normally but use DIFFERENT specific numeric ranges.
scope_restrictions: Population-level general guidance only; never an individual diagnostic boundary.
contradictions_discovered: Genuine 3-way numeric range disagreement (OWH 24-38 vs NICHD 21-35/21-45 vs ACOG 21-45/21-35). The corrected proposition avoids stating a bare number, which resolves the risk; it is eligible for production ONLY in this attributed, source-qualified form. A version that surfaces a single bare number without naming its source would NOT be verified.
reviewer_notes: Correction (HEALTH_SAFETY_EVIDENCE_CORRECTIONS.csv) is sound and independently confirmed necessary.

current_proposition: Menstrual bleeding commonly lasts several days. Bleeding that is unusually prolonged for the user, especially beyond the source's warning threshold, should prompt clinical review rather than an app diagnosis.
independent_corroborating_source: NHS 'Periods' (nhs.uk/conditions/periods/) - heavy bleeding defined as >7 days or >=80ml; period usually ~5 days
relevant_section_heading_locator: Heavy bleeding → When to call the doctor: period lasting longer than eight days
evidence_summary: OWH: 'period lasts longer than eight days' -> call the doctor. NICHD: 'average menstruation time... about 5 days.' NHS independently: periods usually ~5 days (range 2-7), heavy bleeding defined as lasting >7 days.
scope_restrictions: Escalation/education threshold, not a diagnosis. Threshold value is source-specific (8 days in OWH vs NHS's 7-day heavy-bleeding definition).
contradictions_discovered: Minor cross-source day-count variation (7 vs 8 days) between OWH's call-the-doctor threshold and NHS's heavy-bleeding definition -- not a material contradiction since they answer slightly different questions, but worth noting if a single hardcoded day-count is ever surfaced.
reviewer_notes: Proposition wording already avoids stating a bare universal day count outside its own source's framing.

current_proposition: Cycle length can vary between people and from month to month. A new or marked change from a user's established pattern may deserve clinical review.
independent_corroborating_source: OWH_PERIOD (same publisher, companion page) -- irregular-periods when-to-call-the-doctor section
relevant_section_heading_locator: Section: How long is a typical menstrual cycle?
evidence_summary: OWH_CYCLE establishes normal variation; OWH_PERIOD gives the exact 'irregular periods after having normal cycles' escalation criterion.
scope_restrictions: General guidance; a change FROM an established personal pattern, not a fixed universal number.

current_proposition: If periods become irregular after previously being regular, or repeatedly fall outside the source's usual interval, Niswah should recommend discussing the change with a clinician.
independent_corroborating_source: (same OWH_PERIOD page provides both the general and the numeric criterion)
relevant_section_heading_locator: Irregular periods → When to call the doctor
evidence_summary: OWH_PERIOD verbatim: 'You get irregular periods after having normal cycles' and 'Your period happens more often than every 24 days or less often than every 38 days' -> call the doctor.
scope_restrictions: Escalation guidance, not diagnosis. Numeric boundary (24/38 days) is this source's own boundary, distinct from the general-population-range figures in HL-MENS-002.
contradictions_discovered: None -- this is a different, correctly-scoped numeric claim from HL-MENS-002's population-range claim; the KB should keep them distinct.

current_proposition: Heavy bleeding that rapidly soaks menstrual products, lasts unusually long, involves large clots, or is accompanied by dizziness, weakness, chest pain, or breathing difficulty requires medical attention; chest pain or breathing difficulty raises urgency.
independent_corroborating_source: NHS 'Periods' -- soaking pad/tampon hourly, clots bigger than a 50p coin, needing double protection
relevant_section_heading_locator: Heavy bleeding → When to call the doctor
evidence_summary: OWH_PERIOD verbatim covers soaking products, large clots, dizziness/weakness/chest pain/breathing difficulty. NHS independently corroborates with comparable (not identical) thresholds (hourly soaking, coin-sized clots).
contradictions_discovered: None material. Corrected version rightly removed CDC_WARN as secondary since that CDC page is pregnancy/postpartum-scoped -- confirmed appropriate: this session's own CDC_WARN fetch never mentions ordinary (non-pregnant) menstrual bleeding.

current_proposition: Repeated spotting or bleeding between periods is not something the app should diagnose; Niswah should recommend clinical evaluation.
independent_corroborating_source: (none listed; single-source claim, directly verbatim from OWH)
relevant_section_heading_locator: Unusual (abnormal) bleeding → When to see the doctor
evidence_summary: OWH_PERIOD verbatim: 'Spotting or bleeding anytime in the menstrual cycle other than during your period' -> see the doctor.
scope_restrictions: Recommends clinical evaluation; does not diagnose cause.

current_proposition: Bleeding after sex that happens more than once should be discussed with a clinician.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Unusual (abnormal) bleeding → When to see the doctor
evidence_summary: OWH_PERIOD verbatim: 'Bleeding after sex, more than once' -> see the doctor.
scope_restrictions: Repeated occurrence specifically (matches 'more than once' exactly).

current_proposition: Period pain that is severe, persists despite usual over-the-counter measures, or interferes with school, work, or normal activities should prompt clinical evaluation.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Menstrual pain (dysmenorrhea) → When to see your doctor
evidence_summary: OWH_PERIOD verbatim: OTC pain medicine ineffective, or 'the pain interferes with daily activities' -> see your doctor.

current_proposition: Tracking cycle start dates, duration, bleeding pattern, pain, and other symptoms can help a user describe patterns to a clinician; tracking does not itself establish a diagnosis.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Section: Why should I keep track of my menstrual cycle?
evidence_summary: OWH_CYCLE 'why track your cycle' section supports tracking's descriptive/communicative value; source never claims tracking itself is diagnostic.

current_proposition: If a user has missed three periods in a row and is not pregnant or breastfeeding, Niswah should recommend medical evaluation rather than infer the cause.
independent_corroborating_source: (none listed; OWH also gives 2 further age-based triggers not covered by this atom, which is fine as a scoped subset)
relevant_section_heading_locator: Missing periods (amenorrhea) → When to call the doctor
evidence_summary: OWH_PERIOD verbatim: 'You have gone three months without a period and are not pregnant or breastfeeding' -> call the doctor.
scope_restrictions: Scoped to the 3-months-no-period case only; OWH's age-based amenorrhea triggers (age 15/13) are a separate, uncovered case -- not a contradiction, just narrower scope than the full source.
reviewer_notes: Exact match for the case it covers.

current_proposition: Predicted period or fertile dates are estimates based on recorded patterns. Irregular cycles reduce confidence, and predicted dates must never be presented as observed events.
independent_corroborating_source: OWH_TTC (fertility awareness methods, all framed as estimates)
relevant_section_heading_locator: Why should I keep track of my menstrual cycle?
evidence_summary: OWH_CYCLE tracking-purpose section plus OWH_TTC's fertility-awareness methods are consistently framed as predictive/estimated, never certain.

current_proposition: Heavy menstrual bleeding can sometimes be associated with an underlying bleeding disorder. Niswah should not diagnose one, but persistent heavy bleeding should be medically assessed.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Heavy bleeding → causes (bleeding disorders) and when to call the doctor
evidence_summary: OWH_PERIOD verbatim (confirmed via direct re-fetch): 'Hemophilia and von Willebrand's disease are inherited bleeding disorders that cause heavy bleeding during periods.' Located on the same 'Period problems' page cited.
scope_restrictions: Associative statement only ('can sometimes be associated with'), explicitly not a diagnosis -- matches source's own non-diagnostic framing.
contradictions_discovered: None. (Initial locator concern from a partial first fetch was resolved by a targeted verbatim re-fetch of the same page.)

current_proposition: When pregnancy is possible or confirmed, vaginal bleeding must not be handled as ordinary period-tracking data alone. Even spotting in pregnancy should be discussed with a clinician; heavier bleeding follows the urgent maternal-warning pathway.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Missing periods → pregnancy: spotting during pregnancy should be seen by a doctor/nurse
evidence_summary: OWH_PERIOD verbatim (re-fetched): 'If you have spotting during pregnancy you should see your doctor or nurse to be sure.' CDC_WARN verbatim: 'You have any bleeding from your vagina that is more than spotting -- like a period' is an urgent warning sign.
scope_restrictions: Correctly distinguishes spotting (see clinician) from heavier bleeding (urgent pathway) -- matches both sources' own distinction exactly.
reviewer_notes: Exact match, both clauses independently verified verbatim.

current_proposition: Niswah may describe recorded bleeding patterns and explain general health information, but it must not diagnose the medical cause of abnormal bleeding.
independent_corroborating_source: (policy/behavior statement, not an external medical claim)
relevant_section_heading_locator: Page-level disclaimer and sections showing multiple possible causes of irregular/heavy/unusual bleeding
evidence_summary: OWH_PERIOD page lists multiple distinct possible causes across different bleeding patterns (hormonal, structural, bleeding disorders, pregnancy-related) without resolving to one cause -- supports 'must not diagnose the cause.'
scope_restrictions: Restricts app behavior; does not itself assert a clinical fact.

current_proposition: The fertile window is the part of the cycle when intercourse is more likely to result in pregnancy because it falls around ovulation.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Fertility awareness: The menstrual cycle / Charting your fertility pattern
evidence_summary: OWH_TTC verbatim: most fertile '2 to 3 days before ovulation and 12 to 24 hours after.'

current_proposition: A Niswah fertile-window date is an estimate derived from cycle information. It does not confirm that ovulation occurred on a specific day.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Fertility awareness and charting methods; BBT section states temperature rise does not show exactly when the egg is released
evidence_summary: OWH_TTC: BBT rise is retrospective/indirect (typical rise only 0.4-0.8F, confirmed after the fact) -- consistent with 'does not confirm ovulation occurred on a specific day.'
reviewer_notes: Reasonable paraphrase of source's indirect-signal framing, not a verbatim quote.

current_proposition: The timing before ovulation varies between women and can vary from month to month in the same woman, so Niswah should avoid treating a predicted ovulation day as certain.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Fertility awareness: The menstrual cycle
evidence_summary: OWH_TTC describes several distinct fertility-awareness methods, each requiring 8-12 months tracking (calendar method) or acknowledging reduced reliability in some situations -- consistent with ovulation-timing variability.
reviewer_notes: Inference from multiple method-limitation statements, not one single verbatim sentence.

current_proposition: Because sperm can remain capable of fertilization for several days in the reproductive tract, conception can occur from intercourse before ovulation.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Basal body temperature method: sperm can live for up to three days in the source
evidence_summary: OWH_TTC verbatim: 'A man's sperm can live for up to three days in a woman's body. The sperm can fertilize an egg at any point during that time.'
reviewer_notes: Draft's 'several days' is a fair paraphrase of 'up to three days.'

current_proposition: The egg is available for fertilization for a limited time after ovulation. Niswah should use this only as general education, not as an exact personal countdown.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Basal body temperature method: source describes highest fertility around ovulation and 12–24 hours after
evidence_summary: OWH_TTC verbatim: 'almost all women have ovulated within three days after their temperatures spike'; highest fertility 'around ovulation and 12 to 24 hours after.'
scope_restrictions: General education, explicitly not a personal countdown per the atom's own wording.

current_proposition: Calendar-based fertility estimation uses previous cycle lengths and becomes less dependable when cycles vary. It should be combined with other information rather than treated as proof of ovulation.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Charting your fertility pattern → Calendar method
evidence_summary: OWH_TTC verbatim: calendar method needs 'eight to 12 months' of cycle tracking and uses a formula based on shortest/longest cycles -- reliability depends on cycle regularity.

current_proposition: Changes in cervical mucus can be used as a fertility-awareness signal. The method can be less reliable in situations identified by the source, so Niswah should present it as one tracking signal rather than certainty.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Charting your fertility pattern → Cervical mucus method
evidence_summary: OWH_TTC verbatim: cervical mucus method is 'less reliable for some women' including those breastfeeding or using hormonal contraception.
reviewer_notes: Corrected wording (removing an unsupported stronger claim) verified accurate.

current_proposition: A rise in basal body temperature is an indirect sign associated with ovulation and does not identify the exact moment the egg was released.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Charting your fertility pattern → Basal body temperature method
evidence_summary: OWH_TTC BBT section: temperature rise ('only 0.4 to 0.8 degrees F') is an indirect, retrospective sign.

current_proposition: Ovulation predictor kits detect a luteinizing-hormone surge associated with ovulation and can help estimate fertile timing.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Charting your fertility pattern → ovulation kits detect luteinizing-hormone surges
evidence_summary: OWH_TTC verbatim: kits 'detect surges in a specific hormone called luteinizing hormone, which triggers ovulation.'
reviewer_notes: Corrected wording (removing unsupported no-guarantee elaboration) verified as the accurate, source-supported version.

current_proposition: For a woman younger than 35 who has had regular unprotected intercourse for one year without pregnancy, Niswah should suggest discussing fertility evaluation with a clinician.
authoritative_source: When should I consult a health care provider? - NICHD_INF
independent_corroborating_source: ASRM Practice Committee Opinion 'Fertility evaluation of infertile women' (2021) AND ACOG (both independently confirm same 12-month/<35 threshold)
relevant_section_heading_locator: Whole page: one year without successful pregnancy
evidence_summary: NICHD verbatim: 'consult with a health care provider... if they have had unprotected sex for 1 year without a successful pregnancy.' ASRM: 'Evaluation... at 12 months in women <35.' ACOG aligns with the same standard.
scope_restrictions: General referral-timing guidance, not a diagnosis.
reviewer_notes: Strongest-evidenced atom in the TTC category.

current_proposition: For a woman older than 35 who has tried for six months without pregnancy, Niswah should suggest fertility evaluation rather than waiting a full year.
authoritative_source: When should I consult a health care provider? - NICHD_INF
independent_corroborating_source: ASRM ('6 months in women aged >=35') AND ACOG ('women older than 35... after 6 months')
relevant_section_heading_locator: Exceptions: women older than 35 after six months
evidence_summary: NICHD verbatim: 'Women older than age 35 who have had 6 months of unprotected sex.' ASRM/ACOG both independently confirm the 6-month/35 threshold.
contradictions_discovered: Minor boundary-phrasing difference: ASRM phrases the exception as '>=35' (inclusive of exactly 35) while NICHD/ACOG phrase it as 'older than 35' (exclusive). Immaterial for practical guidance but worth naming if the app ever needs the exact-age-35 edge case.
reviewer_notes: Corrected wording ('older than 35') matches NICHD's and ACOG's phrasing exactly; verified as the more precise of the two options.

current_proposition: Earlier fertility evaluation may be appropriate when there are known fertility-affecting conditions or markedly irregular periods.
authoritative_source: When should I consult a health care provider? - NICHD_INF
relevant_section_heading_locator: Exceptions: suspected underlying fertility problems, including irregular periods
evidence_summary: NICHD verbatim: exceptions include 'women who suspect they may have underlying problems... such as irregular periods' and 'individuals... diagnosed with specific conditions.'

current_proposition: Fertility problems can involve the female partner, the male partner, both partners, or remain unexplained. Niswah should avoid framing infertility as solely a woman's issue.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Infertility section: female, male, both/no cause; testing both partners
evidence_summary: OWH_TTC verbatim: 'About one-third of the time, it is a female problem. In another one-third... the man... For the remaining one-third, both partners... or no cause is found'; 'doctor will need to test both you and your partner.'
scope_restrictions: General education, avoids placing sole blame on the woman.

current_proposition: Niswah must not convert a fertile-window estimate into a promise of conception or an unsupported personal pregnancy probability.
independent_corroborating_source: (policy statement, grounded in all TTC method sources above)
relevant_section_heading_locator: Fertility-awareness methods describe likelihood/timing rather than guarantees
evidence_summary: Every fertility-awareness method described by OWH_TTC is framed as an estimate/likelihood, never a guarantee -- supports this behavioral restriction directly.
reviewer_notes: Safe by construction, grounded in the cumulative TTC source material.

current_proposition: Pregnancy dating is commonly counted from the first day of the last normal menstrual period, with pregnancy lasting about 40 weeks.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Introductory paragraph
evidence_summary: OWH_STAGES verbatim: 'Pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks, counting from the first day of your last normal period.'

current_proposition: For educational display, Niswah may group pregnancy into the source's three trimesters: weeks 1–12, 13–28, and 29–40.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Headings: First trimester / Second trimester / Third trimester
evidence_summary: OWH_STAGES verbatim headings: 'First trimester' (week 1-12), 'Second trimester' (13-28), 'Third trimester' (29-40).

current_proposition: Common first-trimester changes can include fatigue, breast tenderness, nausea, mood changes, constipation, frequent urination, headache, and heartburn. Their presence or absence does not confirm that a pregnancy is healthy.
relevant_section_heading_locator: First trimester
evidence_summary: OWH_STAGES lists first-trimester changes including tiredness, breast tenderness, morning sickness, mood swings, constipation, frequent urination, headache, heartburn -- draft's list is an accurate subset.
scope_restrictions: Educational list; presence/absence framing is a safe, non-contradicted addition.

current_proposition: Niswah should encourage early and regular prenatal care; app guidance is not a substitute for prenatal checkups and screening.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Introduction and Prenatal checkups
evidence_summary: OWH_PRENATAL verbatim: regular care 'can help keep you and your baby healthy, spot problems if they occur, and prevent problems during delivery.'
scope_restrictions: General encouragement, not a substitute claim beyond what source supports.

current_proposition: Any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy should be taken seriously and discussed with a clinician. Bleeding that is more than spotting, or bleeding with other urgent warning signs, should follow the urgent maternal-warning pathway.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Missing periods → pregnancy: spotting during pregnancy should be seen by a doctor/nurse
evidence_summary: OWH_PERIOD verbatim (re-fetched): 'If you have spotting during pregnancy you should see your doctor or nurse to be sure.' CDC_WARN verbatim: bleeding 'more than spotting' is an urgent sign.
scope_restrictions: Correctly distinguishes spotting from heavier bleeding.
reviewer_notes: Both source clauses independently verified verbatim this pass.

current_proposition: Pregnancy bleeding can have different causes, some serious. Niswah should not diagnose the cause from chat or tracking data alone and should direct the user to appropriate clinical assessment.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Heavy bleeding → pregnancy problems; missing periods → pregnancy spotting
evidence_summary: Multiple distinct causes of pregnancy bleeding appear across OWH_PERIOD's sections (structural, hormonal, disorder-related) without the source resolving to a single cause.

current_proposition: Pregnancy bleeding accompanied by severe abdominal pain, fainting, severe dizziness, chest pain, or trouble breathing requires urgent medical evaluation.
authoritative_source: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms - CDC_WARN
independent_corroborating_source: (single primary source, CDC's own combined warning-sign list)
relevant_section_heading_locator: Warning signs: dizziness/fainting, chest pain, trouble breathing, severe belly pain, vaginal bleeding
evidence_summary: CDC_WARN verbatim lists severe belly pain, dizziness/fainting, chest pain, and trouble breathing as separate but co-occurring urgent signs.

current_proposition: Bleeding more than spotting at any stage of pregnancy is an urgent maternal warning sign in the CDC source and should not be handled as routine cycle information.
authoritative_source: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms - CDC_WARN
relevant_section_heading_locator: Vaginal bleeding or fluid leaking during pregnancy
evidence_summary: CDC_WARN verbatim: 'You have any bleeding from your vagina that is more than spotting -- like a period' -- listed as an urgent sign without a trimester qualifier.
scope_restrictions: Applies across pregnancy generally per the source's own unqualified phrasing.

current_proposition: Niswah should recognize the CDC urgent maternal warning signs during pregnancy and route them to immediate medical care rather than continuing ordinary educational chat.
authoritative_source: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms - CDC_WARN
relevant_section_heading_locator: Key points and Signs and symptoms
evidence_summary: CDC_WARN full 15-item list independently confirmed this session (see audit notes); page frames these as needing prompt provider contact.
contradictions_discovered: See general note below: 2 of CDC's own 15 listed signs (leg/arm swelling-redness-pain; overwhelming tiredness) are not represented by any atom in this 74-atom set -- a completeness gap in the atom set, not an error in this atom's own claim.
reviewer_notes: Atom's own claim is accurate; flagging KB completeness gap separately.

current_proposition: If a user reports that the baby's movement has stopped or is noticeably less than before, Niswah should advise prompt medical assessment; the app should not use a fixed movement count as a diagnostic rule.
authoritative_source: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms - CDC_WARN
relevant_section_heading_locator: Baby’s movement stopping or slowing during pregnancy
evidence_summary: CDC_WARN verbatim: "Baby's movement stopping or slowing during pregnancy" -- listed without a specific numeric kick-count threshold.
scope_restrictions: Matches 'should not use a fixed movement count as a diagnostic rule' exactly (source itself gives no fixed count).

current_proposition: During pregnancy, users should check prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines, herbs, and supplements with a clinician before starting or stopping them. Stopping a needed medicine can also be harmful.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Using medicine and herbs
evidence_summary: OWH_PREG_SAFE verbatim: 'Always speak with your doctor before you start or stop any medicine'; 'Not using medicine that you need may be more harmful to you and your baby than using the medicine.'

current_proposition: For Saudi-market preconception guidance, the Saudi Ministry of Health recommends 400 micrograms of folic acid daily before pregnancy and through the 12th week of pregnancy; higher-dose use for specified risk conditions should follow clinician guidance.
independent_corroborating_source: CDC Folic Acid (cdc.gov/folic-acid) independently confirms 400 mcg as the general US recommendation
relevant_section_heading_locator: How much folic acid do women need? / Preconception health
evidence_summary: Content independently re-verified this session by fetching the Saudi MOH 'Planning for Pregnancy' page directly: confirms verbatim '400 micrograms (mcg) of folic acid... daily before and during pregnancy (until the 12th week)' and '5 mg' for epilepsy/diabetes/prior neural-tube-defect pregnancy.
scope_restrictions: Saudi-market localization, explicitly scoped as such in the corrected wording.

The claim IS independently confirmed true and on-domain, but via a DIFFERENT, working MOH URL found this session: https://www.moh.gov.sa/en/HealthAwareness/EducationalContent/wh/Pages/008.aspx ("Planning for Pregnancy") -- confirmed reachable (HTTP 301 -> 200) and contains the exact cited content verbatim.
reviewer_notes: RECOMMEND: replace the source_registry_additions.csv URL for SAUDI_MOH_PRECON with the working URL above before this citation is shown to any user.

current_proposition: An app-calculated pregnancy week or due-date estimate is a dating estimate based on available information; it does not confirm fetal development, location, or viability.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Pregnancy counted from last normal period; stage descriptions
evidence_summary: OWH_STAGES frames pregnancy dating as counted/calculated from LMP -- consistent with 'a dating estimate,' and the source never claims this confirms fetal development, location, or viability.

current_proposition: If Niswah receives a high-risk pregnancy flag or the user reports a serious warning symptom, the AI should lower its threshold for directing the user to professional care and must not convert the flag into a diagnosis.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Prenatal provider/checkups: high-risk pregnancies need more frequent/appropriate care
evidence_summary: OWH_PRENATAL verbatim: 'Women with high-risk pregnancies need prenatal care more often and sometimes from a specially trained doctor.' CDC_WARN independently corroborates the general escalation-threshold-lowering framing.

current_proposition: After birth, vaginal discharge called lochia contains blood and tissue from the uterus. It is heavier and redder at first and normally becomes lighter in flow and color over the following weeks.
relevant_section_heading_locator: Physical changes → lochia
evidence_summary: OWH_RECOVERY verbatim: lochia 'is the tissue and blood that lined your uterus'; 'heavy and bright red at first, becoming lighter in flow and color until it goes away after a few weeks.'
reviewer_notes: Close match ('over the following weeks' vs source's 'after a few weeks' -- same meaning).

current_proposition: Postpartum heavy bleeding that soaks one or more pads in an hour, passage of clots larger than an egg or tissue, or foul-smelling discharge is an urgent maternal warning sign.
authoritative_source: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms - CDC_WARN
independent_corroborating_source: (single primary source, CDC's own dedicated bullet)
relevant_section_heading_locator: Vaginal bleeding or discharge after pregnancy
evidence_summary: CDC_WARN verbatim (re-fetched): 'You have heavy bleeding -- soaking through one or more pads in an hour. You pass clots bigger than an egg or you pass tissue. You have vaginal discharge that smells bad.'
reviewer_notes: Exact verbatim match on all three specific details (egg-size clots, foul odor, hourly soaking) -- upgraded from an initial general match to a fully verbatim-confirmed one after a targeted re-fetch.

current_proposition: A severe, sudden, persistent, or worsening headache during pregnancy or within a year after delivery is an urgent maternal warning sign, especially when accompanied by vision changes or dizziness.
authoritative_source: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms - CDC_WARN
relevant_section_heading_locator: Headache that won’t go away or gets worse over time
evidence_summary: CDC_WARN verbatim: 'Headache that won't go away or gets worse over time,' including 'worst headache of your life,' listed alongside vision-change and dizziness signs.
scope_restrictions: Urgent sign, applies pregnancy through year-after-delivery per CDC's general timeframe statement.

current_proposition: A temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher during pregnancy or the postpartum period is an urgent maternal warning sign and should prompt immediate medical care.
authoritative_source: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms - CDC_WARN
relevant_section_heading_locator: Fever of 100.4°F or higher
evidence_summary: CDC_WARN verbatim: 'Fever of 100.4 F or higher.' 100.4F converts exactly to 38.0C.
reviewer_notes: Unit conversion independently checked and correct, not invented.

current_proposition: Chest pain, pressure, a racing or irregular heartbeat, especially with dizziness or breathing difficulty, is an urgent maternal warning sign.
authoritative_source: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms - CDC_WARN
relevant_section_heading_locator: Chest pain or fast-beating heart
evidence_summary: CDC_WARN verbatim: 'Chest pain or fast-beating heart' -- tightness, pressure, irregular heartbeat.

current_proposition: New or worsening trouble breathing during pregnancy or postpartum requires urgent medical care.
authoritative_source: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms - CDC_WARN
relevant_section_heading_locator: Trouble Breathing
evidence_summary: CDC_WARN verbatim: 'Trouble Breathing' -- sudden or gradual shortness of breath.

current_proposition: Severe abdominal pain that is sudden, persistent, or worsening during pregnancy or postpartum is an urgent maternal warning sign.
authoritative_source: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms - CDC_WARN
relevant_section_heading_locator: Severe belly pain that doesn’t go away
evidence_summary: CDC_WARN verbatim: 'Severe belly pain that doesn't go away' -- sudden, persistent, or worsening.

current_proposition: Brief 'baby blues' can occur in the days after birth, but sadness, anxiety, hopelessness, or other depressive symptoms that persist beyond about two weeks or interfere with daily functioning should be discussed with a health professional.
relevant_section_heading_locator: What is postpartum depression? / difference between baby blues and postpartum depression / when to call
evidence_summary: OWH_PPD verbatim: baby blues 'usually go away within a few days'; PPD symptoms 'last longer, are more severe' and note 'longer than 2 weeks' as the differentiator.
reviewer_notes: Matches; 'about two weeks' framing is accurate.

current_proposition: Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby require immediate safety escalation and urgent professional help.
relevant_section_heading_locator: How do I know if I have postpartum depression? / What should I do?
evidence_summary: OWH_PPD verbatim: 'Possible thoughts of harming the baby or yourself' listed as a symptom requiring immediate professional intervention. CDC_WARN independently lists 'Thoughts about harming yourself or your baby.'

current_proposition: Pregnancy-related complications can occur after delivery, including during the year after pregnancy. Niswah's safety checks should remain active throughout that period.
authoritative_source: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms - CDC_WARN
